title: Feature Engineering & Selection
summary: Learn the practical craft of turning raw data into model-ready features — encoding, scaling, missing data, interactions — and how to decide which features are worth keeping.

slides.markdown:
**Feature engineering** is turning raw signals into inputs a model can actually use; **feature selection** is deciding which of those inputs are worth keeping. Together they often move accuracy more than switching from one algorithm to a fancier one.

The craft spans encoding categories, scaling, filling gaps, building interaction terms, and pruning down to what's genuinely predictive — each with its own failure modes, especially **leakage**.

slides.subTitle: Why features often matter more than model choice
slides.markdown:
Swapping logistic regression for a gradient-boosted tree might buy you a couple points of accuracy. Turning a raw `timestamp` into `hour_of_day`, `is_weekend`, and `days_since_last_purchase` can be the difference between a model that can't see a pattern and one that nails it — no model learns a signal that isn't in the data it's given.

This is why practitioners say **"garbage in, garbage out"**, and why strong solutions usually differ more in feature engineering than in model architecture. Model choice fits the signal you hand it; features decide how much signal exists to fit.

slides.subTitle: Encoding categorical variables
slides.markdown:
**One-hot encoding** makes a binary column per category — safe, but explodes in width past a few dozen categories. **Ordinal encoding** maps categories to integers (`low=0, medium=1, high=2`) — valid only when there's a real order, otherwise the model invents a false one. **Target encoding** replaces a category with its average target value — compact even for high-cardinality columns like `zip_code`, but it leaks the label unless done with cross-validation folds or smoothing.

Embeddings (learned dense vectors) generalize target encoding for very high-cardinality columns in deep models.

slides.subTitle: Scaling and normalization
slides.markdown:
**Standardization** (`(x - mean) / std`) centers data at 0 with unit variance — the usual default. **Min-max scaling** (`(x - min) / (max - min)`) squashes values into `[0,1]` — good for a bounded range, but sensitive to outliers skewing the min/max.

Who needs this: **distance-based** models (KNN, SVM, k-means) and **gradient-descent** models (linear/logistic regression, neural nets) — unscaled features let large-magnitude columns dominate. **Tree-based** models (random forest, XGBoost) split per-feature thresholds independently, so scaling changes nothing for them.

slides.subTitle: Handling missing data
slides.markdown:
Simple imputation — mean/median for numeric, mode for categorical — is fast but silently distorts variance and correlations. More robust: **model-based imputation** (predict the missing value from other columns) or a domain-aware default.

The underrated move: add a binary `was_missing` flag alongside the imputed value. Missingness is often **not random** — a skipped income field, an unset optional survey answer — and that pattern itself can be predictive. Dropping rows is only safe when missing values are a tiny, truly random slice.

slides.subTitle: Feature crosses and interaction terms
slides.markdown:
A **feature cross** combines two features so the model can learn effects that only show up in combination — `city x day_of_week` captures that traffic in NYC on Friday behaves differently than either alone predicts. Linear models can't discover this on their own; you hand it to them as a new column or product term.

Tree-based models approximate some interactions via successive splits, but explicit crosses still help them find sharp, known interactions faster. The risk: crossing two high-cardinality columns multiplies cardinality and can overfit fast — cross deliberately, not exhaustively.

slides.subTitle: Feature selection methods
slides.markdown:
**Filter methods** score each feature against the target independently (correlation, chi-squared, mutual information) — fast, but blind to interactions. **Wrapper methods** (forward selection, recursive elimination) retrain a model on different subsets and keep what improves validation score — accurate but expensive. **Embedded methods** build selection into training — **L1 (Lasso)** shrinks unhelpful coefficients to exactly zero as a side effect of fitting.

In practice: filter out the obviously useless, then let an embedded method or tree importances do the fine pruning.

slides.subTitle: Tree-based vs linear/distance-based models
slides.markdown:
| Concern | Tree-based (RF, XGBoost) | Linear / distance-based |
|---|---|---|
| Scaling | Not needed | Required |
| Interactions | Learned via splits | Must be hand-crossed |
| Missing values | Many implementations handle natively | Must impute first |
| Categorical encoding | Can often use raw categories | Needs explicit encoding |

Trees absorb a lot of raw-data mess automatically, a strong default on messy tabular data. Linear and distance-based models are more transparent and can be more accurate once features are well-engineered — but they demand you do that engineering yourself first.

slides.subTitle: Fitting a scaler or encoder before splitting
slides.markdown:
Calling `scaler.fit(X)` or computing target-encoding means on the **whole dataset**, then splitting into train/test, leaks test-set information into training — the scaler's mean/std and the encoder's category averages were computed partly from data the model should never see.

The fix: **split first**, then `fit` the scaler/encoder only on the training fold, and `transform` (never re-fit) the test fold with those same fitted parameters. It's the same class of mistake as computing global statistics before a split anywhere else — small, easy to miss, and it quietly inflates reported metrics.
